Q-Learning.name: Q-Learning
Q-Learning.description: A simple tabular reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the value of actions in states.

sections.whatIsIt: Q-Learning learns a Q-function Q(s,a) that estimates the expected cumulative reward of taking action 'a' in state 's' and following the optimal policy thereafter. During training, the agent explores the environment using an ε-greedy policy to balance exploration and exploitation. After training, the learned (estimated!) Q-values can be used to derive an optimal policy by selecting the action with the highest Q-value in each state (greedy policy). Because it stores one value per state-action pair in a table, Q-Learning needs a small, discrete state space - which is why it is only offered on FrozenLake here.
howItWorks: Take action a, observe reward r and next state s'
Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[target − Q(s,a)], with target = r if the episode ended at s' (terminal states have no future), else r + γ·max Q(s',a')

keyConcepts.Q-Value: Expected cumulative reward for taking action 'a' in state 's'
keyConcepts.Exploration vs Exploitation: Trying random actions to discover new strategies - versus using current knowledge to maximize reward
keyConcepts.Epsilon-Greedy Policy: A policy that chooses a random action with probability ε and the best-known action with probability 1-ε

trainingEpisodes.description: The training budget, counted in episodes. (The deep algorithms count timesteps instead - their episodes vary in length.)

learningRate.description: How much to update Q-values. Higher = faster learning but less stable.

discountFactor.description: Importance of future rewards. Higher = more long-term planning.

explorationRate.description: Probability of random exploration. Higher = more exploration.

qInitialization.description: The table's starting values. Initializing above the true values (optimistic) makes unvisited cells look attractive and drives exploration. Terminal-state entries are never updated and keep their init - the greyed tiles in the Q-table.

links.text: Hugging Face Deep RL Course: Q-Learning (free, hands-on)

DQN.name: DQN (Deep Q-Network)
DQN.description: Q-Learning with a neural network instead of a table: the network estimates Q-values from continuous state inputs, enabling RL in environments where a Q-table is impossible.

sections.whatIsIt: DQN replaces the Q-table with a neural network that takes the state as input and outputs one Q-value per action. This is necessary when states are continuous (like CartPole's positions and velocities): there are infinitely many states, so a table can't hold them. Two tricks make the training stable: a replay buffer stores past experiences and trains the network on random batches of them (breaking the correlation between consecutive steps), and a separate target network provides slowly-changing learning targets. The learning rule is the same Bellman update as Q-Learning, just applied through gradient descent. In RL Lab, DQN also runs on FrozenLake: there the network's Q-values for all 16 states are read out and displayed as the familiar Q-table - the same picture as tabular Q-Learning, produced by a network instead of a table.
howItWorks: Initialize Q-network and target network with random weights
Choose action using ε-greedy policy (ε decays over training)
Take action a, observe reward r and next state s'; store (s, a, r, s') in the replay buffer
Sample a random batch from the buffer and update the Q-network toward r + γ·max Q_target(s',a') (just r for transitions that ended the episode)
Every N steps, copy the Q-network weights into the target network

keyConcepts.Q-Value: Estimated by the neural network: input state, output one Q-value per action
keyConcepts.Replay Buffer: A memory of past experiences; training samples random batches from it - so one lucky success can teach the network thousands of times
keyConcepts.Target Network: A slowly-updated copy of the Q-network that provides stable learning targets - chasing a constantly moving target is what made early deep RL diverge
keyConcepts.Epsilon-Greedy with Decay: Starts fully random (ε = 1) and decays toward exploiting the network estimates as it learns

trainingTimesteps.description: The training budget, counted in environment steps (not episodes - deep-RL convention).

learningRate.description: Step size of the gradient updates to the Q-network. Higher = faster but less stable.

discountFactor.description: Importance of future rewards. Higher = more long-term planning.

explorationFraction.description: Fraction of the timestep budget over which ε decays linearly from 1.0 to its final value.

initialValueEstimate.description: What the untrained network guesses every state is worth. Guessing too high (optimistic) makes unvisited states look attractive and drives exploration even after ε has decayed; guessing too low kills it. The classic “optimistic initial values” trick.

explorationFinalEps.description: Where the decay ends: the exploration that remains for the rest of training. A higher floor keeps the replay buffer diverse.

batchSize.description: How many buffered experiences each gradient step trains on.

links.text: Mnih et al. 2013: Playing Atari with Deep RL (arXiv, free)

PPO.name: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)
PPO.description: Learns the policy directly instead of action values: a neural network outputs action probabilities and is nudged toward actions that worked better than expected. The workhorse of modern RL (robotics, game AI, RLHF for language models).

sections.whatIsIt: Q-Learning and DQN learn how GOOD each action is and derive behavior from that. PPO belongs to the other big family - policy gradients: its network directly outputs the probability of each action, and training shifts probability toward actions that led to better-than-expected returns. A second network (the critic) estimates how good each state is, providing the 'expected' baseline. The 'proximal' part is PPO's safety mechanism: each update may move the policy only a little (the clip range), which keeps training remarkably stable - one reason PPO is the default choice in modern applications, including the RLHF training of language models.
howItWorks: Initialize policy network (actor) and value network (critic)
Collect a batch of experience by acting with the current (stochastic) policy
For each action taken, compute the advantage: did it turn out better or worse than the critic expected?
Increase the probability of better-than-expected actions, decrease worse ones
Clip each update so the new policy stays close to the old one (proximal)
Repeat from step 2 with fresh experience

keyConcepts.Policy: The network's direct output: a probability for each action in the current state
keyConcepts.Advantage: How much better an action turned out compared to the critic's expectation - the learning signal
keyConcepts.Clipping: Updates are limited to a small trusted step (the clip range), preventing destructive policy changes
keyConcepts.Exploration: Comes for free from the stochastic policy - no ε needed. (Though randomness alone does not crack hard-exploration tasks - see MountainCar.)

trainingTimesteps.description: The training budget, counted in environment steps. PPO consumes it in rollouts of fixed size.

learningRate.description: Step size of the gradient updates. Higher = faster but less stable.

discountFactor.description: Importance of future rewards. Higher = more long-term planning.

clipRange.description: How far a single update may move the policy. Smaller = more careful, slower learning.

entropyCoefficient.description: Bonus for keeping the policy random - more exploration, later commitment.

links.text: Schulman et al. 2017: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
